terms.grammar: contrā, preposition with the accusative; mostly with facere
evidence: Tac. Dial. 13.5: necessitāte cotīdiē aliquid contrā animum faciendī
Sen. Const. 19.2: aliquid contrā animum audiendī (Lewis & Short s.v. contrā)
terms.comment: “Against one’s liking”: doing what one would rather not, which is near “against my will” and “against the grain”. Neither this nor Traupman’s phrase says exactly “against what I think wise”.
Traupman’s phrase; not in Lewis & Short or the loci collections. It says “against my character” rather than “against what I think wise”.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.110: invītā Minervā, id est adversante et repugnante nātūrā (Lewis & Short), s.v. invītus
terms.comment: Doing what one has no gift for, not acting against one’s judgment; for “against my will”, mē invītō.

sources: Lewis & Short: adversus · Lewis & Short: ingenium · Lewis & Short: invitus
